title: Quotient Sets and Fibers
---

We return to equivalence relations, now with functions at our disposal. The quotient set $X/{\sim}$ of Definition [1.2.7](/notes/math-55a/1-2-relations#definition-1-2-7) comes with a map from $X$.

:::definition{1.6.1} The quotient map
Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $X$. The ***quotient map*** (or canonical map) of $\sim$ is $$q : X\to X/{\sim}, \qquad q(a) = [a].$$
:::

The quotient map is surjective, since every element of $X/{\sim}$ has the form $[a] = q(a)$. By Lemma [1.2.5](/notes/math-55a/1-2-relations#lemma-1-2-5), $q(a) = q(b)$ if and only if $a\sim b$; so the fiber of $q$ over a class is the class itself, $q^{-1}(\{[a]\}) = [a]$. In particular, $q$ is injective exactly when every class has a single element, that is, when $\sim$ is equality on $X$.

Conversely, every function produces an equivalence relation.

:::proposition{1.6.2} Fibers of a map
Let $f : X\to Y$, and for $a,b\in X$ set $a\sim_f b$ if $f(a) = f(b)$.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. $\sim_f$ is an equivalence relation on $X$, and the class of $a$ is the fiber $f^{-1}(f(a))$. Thus the nonempty fibers $f^{-1}(y)$, $y\in\ran f$, form a partition of $X$.
2. The map $\ol f : X/{\sim_f}\to\ran f$, $[a]\mapsto f(a)$, is well defined and bijective. Its inverse sends $y\in\ran f$ to the fiber $f^{-1}(y)$. In particular, if $f$ is surjective, then $X/{\sim_f}$ is in bijection with $Y$.
:::

:::proof
(a) Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of $\sim_f$ follow from the same properties of equality in $Y$. The class of $a$ is $\{x\in X\mid f(x) = f(a)\} = f^{-1}(f(a))$, and the fiber over $y$ is nonempty exactly when $y\in\ran f$. Proposition [1.2.8](/notes/math-55a/1-2-relations#proposition-1-2-8) shows that the classes form a partition.

(b) The value $f(a)$ depends only on the class $[a]$: if $[a] = [b]$, then $a\sim_f b$, that is, $f(a) = f(b)$. So $\ol f = \{([a],f(a))\mid a\in X\}$ is a function. It is injective, since $f(a) = f(b)$ means $[a] = [b]$, and surjective, since each $y\in\ran f$ is $f(a) = \ol f([a])$ for some $a$. The class sent to $y = f(a)$ is $[a] = f^{-1}(y)$.
:::

Putting the pieces together, three kinds of data on a set carry the same information.

:::theorem{1.6.3} Relations, partitions, and surjections
Let $X$ be a set.

<!-- list:paren-alpha -->

1. Equivalence relations on $X$ correspond to partitions of $X$: an equivalence relation $\sim$ corresponds to $X/{\sim}$, and a partition $\mfC$ to $\sim_{\mfC}$.
2. Every equivalence relation $\sim$ on $X$ is the relation $\sim_q$ determined by a surjection, namely its quotient map $q : X\surjto X/{\sim}$.
3. Every surjection $f : X\surjto Y$ determines the equivalence relation $\sim_f$, whose classes are the fibers of $f$, and $f$ is the quotient map $q : X\to X/{\sim_f}$ followed by the bijection $\ol f : X/{\sim_f}\to Y$; that is, $f = \ol f\circ q$.

So an equivalence relation on $X$, a partition of $X$, and a surjection from $X$ onto another set (up to a bijection of the target) are three descriptions of the same thing.
:::

:::proof
Part (a) is Proposition [1.2.8](/notes/math-55a/1-2-relations#proposition-1-2-8). For (b), $q(a) = q(b)$ if and only if $a\sim b$, by Lemma [1.2.5](/notes/math-55a/1-2-relations#lemma-1-2-5); so $\sim_q$ is $\sim$. For (c), Proposition [1.6.2](/notes/math-55a/1-6-quotient-sets-and-fibers#proposition-1-6-2) shows that $\ol f$ is a bijection onto $\ran f = Y$, and $(\ol f\circ q)(a) = \ol f([a]) = f(a)$ for every $a\in X$.
:::

More generally, given an equivalence relation $\sim$ on $X$ and an arbitrary function $f : X\to Y$, we may ask whether $f$ induces a function on the quotient by the rule $[a]\mapsto f(a)$. The difficulty is that a class $[a]$ has many representatives, and the proposed value must not depend on which one we pick.

:::proposition{1.6.4} Maps descending to a quotient
Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $X$ with quotient map $q : X\to X/{\sim}$, and let $f : X\to Y$. There is a function $\ol f : X/{\sim}\to Y$ with $f = \ol f\circ q$ if and only if $f$ is ***compatible*** with $\sim$, meaning that $$a\sim b \implies f(a) = f(b) \qquad\text{for all } a,b\in X.$$ In that case $\ol f$ is unique, it is given by $\ol f([a]) = f(a)$, and its image is $f(X)$.

![fig-1-6-1](/notes/math-55a/figures/fig-1-6-1.svg)
:::

:::proof
If $\ol f$ exists and $a\sim b$, then $q(a) = q(b)$, so $f(a) = \ol f(q(a)) = \ol f(q(b)) = f(b)$. Conversely, suppose $f$ is compatible with $\sim$, and let $\ol f = \{([a],f(a))\mid a\in X\}\subseteq(X/{\sim})\times Y$. Its domain is $X/{\sim}$, and if two of its pairs $([a],f(a))$ and $([b],f(b))$ have the same first coordinate, then $[a] = [b]$, so $a\sim b$ and $f(a) = f(b)$. Hence $\ol f$ is a function, and $\ol f(q(a)) = \ol f([a]) = f(a)$ for all $a$. It is unique because $q$ is surjective: any $g$ with $f = g\circ q$ satisfies $g([a]) = g(q(a)) = f(a)$ for every class $[a]$. Finally, $\ol f(X/{\sim}) = \{f(a)\mid a\in X\} = f(X)$.
:::

When $f$ is compatible with $\sim$, we say that $f$ ***descends*** to $X/{\sim}$, or ***factors through*** $q$. The diagram above ***commutes***: the two routes from $X$ to $Y$ give the same map. The induced map $\ol f$ is injective if and only if $f(a) = f(b)$ implies $a\sim b$, that is, if and only if $\sim$ is exactly the relation $\sim_f$; and $\ol f$ is surjective if and only if $f$ is. This principle will return many times: quotient groups (Theorem [3.3.2](/notes/math-55a/3-3-the-isomorphism-theorems#theorem-3-3-2)) and quotient vector spaces (Definition [7.1.1](/notes/math-55a/7-1-quotient-spaces#definition-7-1-1)) are built on it. Here is its first use.

:::example{1.6.5} Addition mod $n$
Let $\sim$ be congruence mod $n$ on $\ZZ$ (Example [1.2.9](/notes/math-55a/1-2-relations#example-1-2-9)). We would like to add classes by the rule $[a]+[b] = [a+b]$. For this to make sense, the right side must depend only on the classes $[a]$ and $[b]$, not on the representatives $a$ and $b$. It does: if $a\sim a'$ and $b\sim b'$, then $n$ divides $a'-a$ and $b'-b$, hence their sum $(a'+b')-(a+b)$, so $a+b\sim a'+b'$. In the language of Proposition [1.6.4](/notes/math-55a/1-6-quotient-sets-and-fibers#proposition-1-6-4): for fixed $b$, the map $\ZZ\to\ZZ/{\sim}$, $a\mapsto[a+b]$, is compatible with $\sim$, so it descends to a map $\ZZ/{\sim}\to\ZZ/{\sim}$, $[a]\mapsto[a+b]$; and the result depends only on $[b]$, since $[a+b] = [a+b']$ whenever $b\sim b'$. Hence $$[a]+[b]\coloneqq[a+b]$$ is a well-defined operation on $\ZZ/{\sim}$. Under the bijection $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\to\ZZ/{\sim}$, $r\mapsto[r]$, it becomes addition of remainders: $[a]+[b]$ is the class $[r]$, where $r$ is the remainder of $a+b$ on division by $n$. This is the group $\ZZ/n\ZZ$ of the next chapter (Example [2.2.3](/notes/math-55a/2-2-fundamental-examples#example-2-2-3)), which we describe there as $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with addition mod $n$.
:::
